title: Functional Programming: Pattern Matching & Declarative Style

slides.title: Structural Pattern Matching (match/case)
slides.prompt: Python 3.10 introduced structural pattern matching (`match`/`case`), allowing functional-style data decomposition and branching based on structure rather than verbose if-else ladders.
slides.codeSnippet:
def process_command(command):
    match command.split():
        case ["quit"]:
            return "Exiting"
        case ["go", direction]:
            return f"Heading {direction}"
        case _:
            return "Unknown command"

slides.title: Guards in Structural Pattern Matching
slides.prompt: How do you add an extra condition (guard) to a 'case' statement in Python structural pattern matching?
options: By appending an 'if' clause to the case (e.g., case [x, y] if x == y:)
By placing a nested try-except inside the match block
By wrapping the case in a lambda expression
slides.correctAnswer: By appending an 'if' clause to the case (e.g., case [x, y] if x == y:)

slides.title: Matching Class Instances
slides.prompt: Fill in the match keyword used to evaluate against variable patterns.
slides.codeSnippet:

slides.title: Imperative vs Declarative Style
slides.prompt: Which statement describes the core focus of Declarative (Functional) programming style?
options: Focusing on 'what' to transform rather than explicit step-by-step state modifications ('how')
Focusing on mutating global object properties sequentially inside loops
Writing code without function definitions or parameters
Relying entirely on compile-time type casting
slides.correctAnswer: Focusing on 'what' to transform rather than explicit step-by-step state modifications ('how')
